kurz: How to weigh the one-off tax advantage of a unit-linked policy on the gain against its annual cost disadvantage on the assets.

bloecke.md:
A unit-linked policy is an insurance contract that holds fund units, often the same ETFs that you could also buy yourself. The investment can therefore be the same as in a securities account; the difference lies in the legal construction. The insurer owns the units, and the customer has a claim against the insurer. All the other differences follow from this: the different taxation, the tax-free fund switch, the lifelong pension and additional costs for the insurance contract.

Whether the policy or the securities account is more favourable can therefore be calculated. On one side is a tax advantage that acts once, at the end, on the *gain*. On the other side is a cost disadvantage that acts every year on the *entire assets*. If you put a figure on both, the difference shows which option comes out better.

## Taxation of policy and securities account

The 12/62 rule from Section 20(1) no. 6 EStG (Income Tax Act) applies to the one-off lump-sum payout. If the contract runs for at least twelve years and the money is paid out no earlier than after the 62nd birthday (for contracts from the years 2005 to 2011, the 60th birthday), only half of the difference between the payout and the premiums paid in is taxable. However, this half is taxed at the personal tax rate, because Section 32d(2) no. 2 EStG excludes it from the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer). For a unit-linked policy, there is also a [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] of 15% on the fund income. This makes 0.5 × 0.85 = 42.5% of the gain taxable.

In the securities account, the [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax]] of 25% plus solidarity surcharge is due, 26.375% in total, on 70% of the gain. The partial exemption for equity funds under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) is 30% there instead of 15%. The effective burden is therefore 18.5% of the gain, regardless of income. The solidarity surcharge continues to be levied in full on the capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer), while most income tax payers have not paid it since 2021. This shifts the comparison slightly in favour of the policy.

bloecke.md:
## Reduction in yield as the yardstick

Six percentage points on the gain seems a lot at first. What counts for the comparison is how much in additional annual costs they can offset. The yardstick for this is the [[Reduction in yield (Effektivkosten)|reduction in yield (Effektivkosten)]], which every provider must disclose in the key information document under the PRIIPs rules. It states by how many percentage points the return falls each year because of all the costs of the product, that is, acquisition, administration, fixed per-contract charges, risk costs and the fund TER together. For commission-based unit-linked policies, this figure is roughly between 1.8% and 2.7% a year in the 2025/2026 market overview. That is a range, not official statistics. An ETF savings plan in a securities account is usually below 0.3% including TER.

This gap is considerable and is not offset by a tax advantage. It is a difference between two returns, and differences in return grow exponentially over the term, while the tax advantage depends linearly on the gain.

bloecke.md:
The calculation uses a marginal tax rate of 30% in the year of payout. The reduction in yield of 0.90% for the commission-free policy is an assumption for this illustrative calculation, not a market value. For the securities account, a sale at the end is assumed. The saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) of €1,000 is not taken into account. It would shift the result slightly in favour of the securities account.

These simplifications do not change the ranking. The expensive policy is around €73,000 behind the securities account, and the low-cost commission-free policy is still about €20,000 behind. In both cases the policy saves tax. But it has previously generated a smaller gain, to which the saving relates.

## Break-even calculation

The reverse calculation is more informative than three worked examples. It determines the maximum reduction in yield the policy may have for the end result to be the same as in the securities account. With the previous assumptions (€300 a month, 30 years, 7% gross, securities account with a 0.25% reduction in yield), the limit is narrow.

At a marginal tax rate of 20% in the year of payout, the policy may have a reduction in yield of around 0.7%, at 30% around 0.5% and at 42% only around 0.3%. With these values, it is practically level with the securities account. Depending on the tax rate, the policy's tax advantage therefore offsets only 0.05 to 0.45 percentage points of additional annual costs.

bloecke.unter: Calculated against a securities account with a 0.25% reduction in yield over 30 years; the reference line marks the lower end of the market range for commission-based unit-linked policies.

bloecke.md: The policy's tax advantage is a one-off percentage of the gain. The cost disadvantage is an annual percentage of the entire assets. That is why the cost side almost always decides, and the stated reduction in yield is the first figure to look for in an offer.

## Advance lump sum

The illustrative calculation above does not yet include the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]]. Under Section 18 InvStG, it arises every year in the securities account, but not in the policy. The base interest rate (Basiszins) for 2026 is 3.20%. Of this, 70% is applied, that is, around 2.24% of the fund value at the start of the year, but at most the increase in value that occurred during the year. After 30% partial exemption and 26.375% tax, around 0.41% of the portfolio value thus flows out each year. As long as the saver's allowance of €1,000 is sufficient, no tax is due on it. In 2026 it covers a portfolio value of about €64,000 if there is no other capital income.

The effect is smaller than it first appears. The advance lump sums applied during the holding period are deducted from the capital gain on a later sale (Section 19(1) InvStG) and thus reduce the tax at the end. All that is lost is the interest on the tax paid early. Compared with a very low-cost commission-free policy, this noticeably reduces the securities account's lead. Compared with a policy with a 2% reduction in yield, it does not change the result.

## Fund switches and early exit

The second argument for the policy is the tax-free fund switch, and it is valid. If the customer reallocates within the contract or restores the target weighting (rebalancing), this does not trigger a disposal, because the customer does not own the units directly. In the securities account, every sale costs tax, and under the FIFO principle it applies first to the oldest units, which have usually accumulated the highest gains. For investors who change their strategy every few years, this is worth a lot. For a buy-and-hold investor with a single world ETF, it is worth nothing, because the investor pays for an option that goes unused.

Exiting the policy, on the other hand, is expensive. For contracts from 2015 onwards, the insurer may charge at most 2.5% of total premiums through the Zillmer adjustment (Zillmerung), that is, offset this amount against the first premiums straight away (maximum Zillmer rate under Section 4 DeckRV, the Actuarial Reserves Ordinance). This limit only applies to the Zillmer adjustment; the agreed acquisition costs can be higher. For the surrender value, they must be spread over the first five years for contracts from 2008 onwards under Section 169 VVG (Insurance Contract Act). This is why the surrender value in the first years is typically below two thirds of the payments. If the contract ends before the 12/62 conditions are met, the taxation of only half the gain also no longer applies. The regular flat-rate withholding tax then applies to 85% of the difference. Including the solidarity surcharge, that is around 22.4%, and thus more than the 18.5% in the securities account.

bloecke.md:
## Annuitisation and the annuity conversion factor

If you choose the lifelong pension instead of the lump-sum payout, the taxation changes completely. Instead of the 12/62 rule, taxation of the income portion under Section 22 no. 1 sentence 3 letter a double letter bb EStG then applies. For a pension starting at 67, 17% of the pension is taxable, for a start at 65 or 66, 18%, and at 63, 20%. With a monthly pension of €1,000 and a 30% marginal tax rate, that is €51 of tax, or around 5% of the pension. In tax terms, this is the policy's strongest point. It is usually overlooked in comparisons with the securities account, because they always consider the lump-sum option. You cannot use both types of taxation at the same time.

The amount of the pension is determined by the annuity conversion factor (Rentenfaktor), that is, the monthly pension per €10,000 of policy value. Offers almost always state two values, a guaranteed one and a higher “current” or “projected” factor. Only the guaranteed one is binding. It is calculated using very cautious mortality tables and is correspondingly low.

bloecke.titel: Guaranteed and current annuity conversion factor
bloecke.md: With a guaranteed annuity conversion factor of 22 and a current one of 30, a policy value of €300,000 yields a monthly pension of €660 instead of €900. The difference of 27% results solely from the choice of factor. The current factor only reflects the present situation and is not binding. Changes to benefits are permitted under the narrow conditions of Section 163 VVG. If a policy is taken out for the sake of annuitisation, the guaranteed factor must be written into the contract. The advisory documents are not sufficient for this.

## Commission-free policy

A commission-free policy contains no built-in acquisition commission. Instead, the advice is paid for separately by a fee. This significantly lowers the stated reduction in yield. Only in this way can a policy reach the break-even calculated above at all.

One problem lies in how the costs are presented. If the fee is derived from the “commission saved” and not included in the stated reduction in yield, the policy appears cheaper than it is. The costs are still incurred; they simply appear on a different invoice. A one-off fee of €3,000 on a 30-year contract with a monthly premium of €300 corresponds to just under 2.8% of total premiums. As an annual reduction in return, this is considerable in the first years, because the fee is incurred early and acts on assets that are still small. For the comparison, what counts is therefore the reduction in yield including the fee.

schritte.text: The figure is in the key information document under the PRIIPs Regulation, not in the advertising brochure. Without it, no comparison is possible, and the check ends here.

schritte.titel: Estimate the marginal tax rate in the year of payout
schritte.text: What matters is the rate in retirement, not today's rate. With the statutory pension and withdrawals as the only income, it is often well below today's rate. A lower rate increases the policy's advantage over the securities account.

If, depending on the marginal tax rate, the reduction in yield is more than around 0.05 to 0.45 percentage points above your own securities account costs, the tax advantage no longer offsets the shortfall over 30 years.

schritte.titel: Add the fee for a net tariff
schritte.text: The fee is spread over the term as an annual amount and added to the reduction in yield. Without this step, two different things are being compared.

schritte.titel: Check the guaranteed annuity conversion factor
schritte.text: This step is only necessary if annuitisation is seriously planned. Otherwise the factor plays no role, and the policy loses its strongest argument.

bloecke.titel: Cases in favour of the policy
bloecke.md:
In three constellations, the policy can come out ahead in arithmetical terms:

- With a genuine commission-free policy with a low reduction in yield and planned annuitisation, the taxable income portion of 17% applies instead of the 12/62 rule. The securities account does not achieve such a low burden in the withdrawal phase.
- With an active strategy involving frequent reallocation, investors continually realise gains in a securities account if they change their fund selection every two to three years or rebalance strictly. The tax deferral in the policy then takes effect with every switch and not just once.
- If the goal is longevity protection rather than return, what counts is the guaranteed lifelong payment. It is an insurance benefit that protects the buyer against a very long life and for which the buyer pays with return. Such a contract must be assessed differently from an investment.

In all other cases, at today's usual cost levels, the securities account comes out better.

The calculation above applies to a new contract. With an existing contract, the acquisition costs have already been paid and cannot be recovered. In the comparison with the securities account, only the future cost burden then counts. Terminating before the 12/62 conditions are met (for contracts from 2005 to 2011: 12/60) also costs the advantage of taxation of only half the gain. Making the policy paid-up or reducing premiums is often the better choice than surrender. Old contracts from before 2005 are tax-free on payout if they meet the conditions applicable at the time, and are therefore practically irreplaceable.

mitnehmen: Because the policy's tax advantage acts once on the gain and the cost disadvantage acts every year on the entire assets, the cost side usually decides.

Under the 12/62 rule, 42.5% of the gain is taxable; in the securities account, 70% is taxed at 26.375%, that is, 18.5% effectively. Depending on the marginal tax rate, the advantage offsets only 0.05 to 0.45 percentage points of additional annual costs.
The 12/62 rule for the lump-sum payout and taxation of the income portion for the lifelong pension are mutually exclusive.
The tax-free fund switch only benefits investors who actually switch their funds.
For the annuity conversion factor, only the guaranteed value counts, because the projected one does not bind the insurer.

begriffe.text: Unit-linked pension or life insurance in which the insurer holds the fund units and the customer has a claim against the insurer. This gives rise to its own taxation, the tax-free fund switch and the costs of the insurance contract in addition to the fund TER.

Key figure in the key information document, known in German as Effektivkosten, that states by how many percentage points a year all product costs reduce the return. It covers acquisition, administration, fixed per-contract charges, risk costs and fund TER together. It is the only reliable yardstick for comparing the costs of a policy and a securities account.

Condition under Section 20(1) no. 6 EStG according to which the contract must run for at least twelve years and the payout must be made no earlier than after the 62nd birthday, or after the 60th birthday for contracts from the years 2005 to 2011. Only half of the difference is then taxable, but at the personal tax rate instead of the flat-rate withholding tax.
Monthly pension per €10,000 of policy value on annuitisation. Only the guaranteed factor is binding. The current or projected factor stated in addition does not bind the insurer.

Policy without a built-in acquisition commission, where the advice is paid for by a fee. It is only comparable with a commission-based policy or a securities account if the fee is included in the cost calculation.

Taxable portion of a private life annuity under Section 22 no. 1 EStG. Depending on age at the start of the pension, it is 17% at 67, 18% at 65 or 66 and 20% at 63. It applies instead of the 12/62 rule, not in addition to it.
